0.0.n: This polite expression gets the staff member’s attention here, rather than apologizing.

1.0.n: Here it acknowledges the customer’s call and invites them to speak.

2.0.n: This noun names the action the customer wants permission to perform.

2.1.n: いい means acceptable; です makes the question polite.

2.2.n: Placed at the end, this makes the sentence a question.

3.0.n: The staff member gives permission to go ahead with the order.

4.0.n: This drawn-out hesitation gives the speaker time to decide what to say.

4.2.n: This borrowed drink name is followed by a choice of serving temperature.

4.3.n: This links the latte to ホット, selecting the hot version of the drink.

4.4.n: This borrowed word functions as a menu option, contrasting with アイス.

5.0.n: The staff member acknowledges the drink choice.

6.0.n: This connects another item to the drink already ordered.

6.2.n: This hesitation fills the pause while the customer chooses the next item.

6.4.n: This borrowed noun introduces the next category in the order.

6.5.n: が marks dessert as the subject; the unfinished phrasing introduces what the dessert choice will be.

6.7.n: 昔ながら describes something retaining its traditional style.

6.8.n: This connects 昔ながら to プリン so the traditional-style description applies to the pudding.

6.9.n: In Japanese, this usually refers to a set custard dessert, often served with caramel.

7.0.n: The staff member acknowledges the dessert choice.

8.0.n: At the start of this sentence, で links the conversation to an additional request.

8.2.n: This politely softens the introduction of another request.

8.4.n: With する, this borrowed noun describes getting food to take away.

8.5.n: This marks takeout as an addition to the order already discussed.

8.6.n: する becomes したい to express desire; its て-form, したくて, leaves the request gently unfinished.

9.0.n: The staff member repeats the customer’s requested service option to confirm it.

9.2.n: This acknowledges that the additional items will be to go.

10.0.n: This borrowed food name identifies the first takeout item.

10.1.n: 個 is a counting word for individual items, used here for a pastry.

11.0.n: The staff member repeats the item name to confirm the order.

11.2.n: This signals that the staff member has registered the item.

12.0.n: This adds another item to the takeout order.

12.2.n: This borrowed compound names the cookie; チョコ is short for チョコレート.

12.3.n: 個 counts individual objects, here specifying a single cookie.

13.0.n: The staff member acknowledges the cookie order.

14.0.n: This names the service option the customer wants for these items.

14.1.n: で marks the requested arrangement: having the items packed to go.

14.2.n: This polite request formula asks the listener to carry out the stated arrangement.

15.0.n: This acknowledges the customer’s final instruction.

15.2.n: This very polite past form of かしこまる is a standard service expression confirming acceptance of a request.

15.4.n: This expresses gratitude and combines with ございます for a polite closing.

15.5.n: ござい is the form of ござる used before ます; here it helps make the thanks formal.

15.6.n: This attaches to ござい, completing ございます and making the expression polite.

0.tip: すみません can politely attract attention, not just express an apology.

1.tip: はい can mean you are listening, rather than agreeing with a statement.

2.tip: 注文いいですか is a compact spoken way to ask permission to order.

3.tip: Here はい gives the customer the go-ahead.

4.tip: Drink name + の + ホット selects the hot version without needing a full sentence.

5.tip: Staff often use はい after each item to show they have heard it.

6.lit: And, um, dessert is old-fashioned custard pudding.
6.tip: 昔ながらの describes something made in a familiar, traditional style.

7.tip: This はい acknowledges the item rather than answering a question.

8.lit: And, excuse me, takeout also wanting to do…
8.tip: Ending with したくて softly introduces a wish while leaving the full request unstated.

9.tip: Repeating the customer’s word is a natural way for staff to confirm they understood.

10.tip: An item name followed by a quantity is enough when placing an order.

11.tip: The Japanese repeats only the item name, not the quantity.

12.lit: And, chocolate chunk cookie, one item.
12.tip: と can start a spoken fragment when adding another item to an order.

13.tip: This short acknowledgment keeps the ordering exchange moving.

14.tip: Option + でお願いします politely requests a particular arrangement.

15.tip: かしこまりました is a particularly polite way for service staff to accept a request.
